{"evidence":[{"sentence_id":0,"text":"\"He Mele Lāhui Hawaiʻ i\" (\"The Song of the Hawaiian Nation\") was composed by Liliuokalani in November 1866 at the request of Kamehameha V, who wanted a national anthem to replace the British anthem \"God Save the King\".","title":"He Mele Lahui Hawaii"},{"sentence_id":1,"text":" It replaced Lunalilo's composition \"E Ola Ke Aliʻ i Ke Akua\" as the national anthem.","title":"He Mele Lahui Hawaii"},{"sentence_id":2,"text":" Liliʻ uokalani wrote: \"The king was present for the purpose of Criticising my new composition of both words and music, and was liberal in his commendations to me on my success.","title":"He Mele Lahui Hawaii"},{"sentence_id":3,"text":" He admired not only the beauty of music, but spoke enthusiastically of the appropriate words, so well adapted to the air and to the purpose for which they were written.","title":"He Mele Lahui Hawaii"},{"sentence_id":4,"text":" This remained in use as our national anthem for some twenty years or more when my brother composed the words \"Hawaiʻ i Ponoʻ ī\".\"","title":"He Mele Lahui Hawaii"},{"sentence_id":0,"text":"\"O Canada\" (French: \"Ô Canada\" ) is the national anthem of Canada.","title":"O Canada"},{"sentence_id":1,"text":" The song was originally commissioned by Lieutenant Governor of Quebec Théodore Robitaille for the 1880 Saint-Jean-Baptiste Day ceremony; Calixa Lavallée composed the music, after which, words were written by the poet and judge Sir Adolphe-Basile Routhier.","title":"O Canada"},{"sentence_id":2,"text":" The lyrics were originally in French; an English version was created in 1906.","title":"O Canada"},{"sentence_id":3,"text":" Robert Stanley Weir wrote in 1908 another English version, which is the official and most popular version, one that is not a literal translation of the French.","title":"O Canada"},{"sentence_id":4,"text":" Weir's lyrics have been revised twice, taking their present form in 1980, but the French lyrics remain unaltered.","title":"O Canada"},{"sentence_id":5,"text":" \"O Canada\" had served as a \"de facto\" national anthem since 1939, officially becoming Canada's national anthem in 1980 when the Act of Parliament making it so received royal assent and became effective on July 1 as part of that year's Dominion Day (now known as Canada Day) celebrations.","title":"O Canada"}],"peer_messages":[],"previous_answer":"noanswer","question":"Vincas Kudirka is the author of both the music and lyrics of a national anthem which has how many words?"}
